q: What is the purpose of solution evaluation?
options: To write the requirements
To assess whether a solution has achieved the desired business results
To identify the stakeholders
To estimate the project budget
explanation: Solution evaluation activities assess whether or not a solution has achieved the desired business results, by comparing actual results with expected values and, over the long term, checking whether the expected business value was achieved.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Solution Evaluation

links.label: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Solution Evaluation

q: Which of these is one of the four solution evaluation processes?
options: Assemble Business Case
Conduct Elicitation
Verify Requirements
Obtain Solution Acceptance for Release
explanation: The four processes are Evaluate Solution Performance, Determine Solution Evaluation Approach, Evaluate Acceptance Results and Address Defects, and Obtain Solution Acceptance for Release.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Table 1-2

links.label: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Table 1-2

q: Why should the solution evaluation approach be defined as early as possible?
options: Because the sponsor signs it before the charter
Because it replaces acceptance criteria
Because some metrics need data the product would not otherwise capture, which is costly or impossible to add later
Because evaluation happens before requirements are written
explanation: Some metrics require capturing information beyond what the product itself needs. Without early definition there is a risk that the necessary information will be expensive or impossible to obtain.

q: What is a metric, in solution evaluation?
options: A set of quantifiable measures used to evaluate a solution or business
A type of stakeholder
A stage of the product life cycle
A kind of prototype
explanation: A metric is a set of quantifiable measures used to evaluate a solution or business. In solution evaluation it defines how solution performance can be quantified.

q: A proposed metric would be too expensive to collect. What should the team do?
options: Skip evaluation altogether
Collect it regardless of cost
Wait until after release to decide
Consider a less costly, next-best alternative
explanation: The cost of capturing and reporting measurements is an important factor. When proposed metrics appear too costly or time-consuming, less costly, next-best alternatives may be considered.

q: In acceptance testing, how is the work divided between testers and business analysis?
options: The business analyst runs all the tests
Testers determine pass or fail; business analysis evaluates the severity, cause and impact of defects and recommends what to do
Testers decide whether to release the product
There is no difference between the two roles
explanation: The pass/fail comparison of results with criteria is typically a testing task. Business analysis then considers the magnitude and severity of the defects, their root cause and risks, and recommends ways to address them.

q: What do "evaluated acceptance results" contain?
options: A comparison of acceptance criteria with actual results, the root cause of variances, the cost to address defects and the business impact
Only a list of passed tests
The project's final budget
The stakeholder register
explanation: Evaluated acceptance results give a summarized comparison between the acceptance criteria and the actual acceptance results, with the root cause for variances or defects, the cost to address them, and the business impact of addressing or accepting them.

q: Two defects are found. One affects a feature tied to the project's top business objective. Which tool shows this link?
options: Onion diagram
Persona
Traceability matrix
Product box
explanation: A traceability matrix can be used to assess the business impact of not addressing defects: there could be a significant impact from defects in features that trace to a high-priority objective.

q: Which is NOT one of the recommendations the guide lists for addressing a defect?
options: A workaround in how the product is used
A modification to the product, possibly through a change request
Communication to users about how the product is meant to be used
Deleting the acceptance criterion so the test passes
explanation: Recommendations may include workarounds, modifications to the product, adjustments to how results are measured, investigation of technical causes, and communication to users. Removing a criterion to hide a failure is not among them.

q: On an adaptive project, a story is demonstrated and does not meet its acceptance criteria. What happens?
options: It is accepted anyway to protect velocity
The story can be rejected and returned to the backlog to be reprioritized
The iteration is extended until it passes
The project is cancelled
explanation: If the demonstration does not prove conformance to the acceptance criteria, the entire story can be rejected and returned to the backlog to be reprioritized. Defects are added to the backlog.

q: Which set lists the bases for a release decision?
options: Acceptable results, organizational readiness, completed transition activities, and acceptance of remaining risks
Budget spent, team size, sponsor's mood, and schedule
Number of requirements, number of tests, number of defects, and number of users
Scope, time, cost and quality
explanation: Release decisions are typically based on the acceptability of the solution, confirmation that the organization is ready, confirmation that transition activities are complete, and acceptance of any remaining product risks and workarounds.

q: Who makes the release decision?
options: The business analyst alone
The test team
The stakeholders accountable for the product, with the analyst facilitating
The newest team member
explanation: Obtaining solution acceptance gives the stakeholders accountable for the product the opportunity to decide whether it should be released in whole, in part or not at all. The process is one of facilitating that decision.

q: What are the possible release decisions?
options: Approve only
Release fully or partly, delay, or disapprove
Verify or validate
Avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept
explanation: A release decision may permit the release or partial release of the solution, delay it, or disapprove and prevent it. It often includes a sign-off.

q: What is a warranty period?
options: The time allowed for writing requirements
The time before the charter is approved
The length of an iteration
A period after release during which the development team is responsible for fixing defects
explanation: A warranty period is an interval of time during which the product development team is responsible for addressing any defects found after the solution is released for production.

q: What technique is recommended for making a release decision, and why?
options: A facilitated workshop, so all stakeholders hear the reasons for the decision
A survey, so nobody has to meet
Observation, so users are not disturbed
A product box, to design the packaging
explanation: Whenever possible, release decisions should be made in a facilitated workshop so that all stakeholders hear the rationale. Summaries of results, remaining risks and unfinished transition activities help decision makers.

q: On an adaptive project, how is acceptance usually obtained at the end of an iteration?
options: A formal sign-off by the PMO
A written contract amendment
The product owner's approval at the demonstration that the work meets the definition of done
It is not obtained
explanation: In adaptive approaches, often verbal approval alone is obtained from the product owner, as part of demonstration and feedback, that the solution segment meets the definition of done and can be released.

q: When does Evaluate Solution Performance usually take place?
options: Before the business case is written
During elicitation
Before any testing
After the solution has been released
explanation: Evaluation of solution performance typically occurs after a solution has been released, so it is more likely to occur during portfolio or program activities than project activities.

q: Sales were 1,000 units a month before the new system and 1,300 after. How is the business value quantified?
options: As the difference between the baseline and the performance after release: 300 units a month
As 1,300 units a month
As 1,000 units a month
It cannot be quantified
explanation: Performance data before a release are the baseline. If value is measured as increased sales volume, the quantified business value is the difference in sales volume before and after release.

q: A business objective cannot be measured directly. What can be used?
options: Nothing; evaluation is skipped
A proxy, such as task duration, response time or error counts
The sponsor's opinion only
The original estimate
explanation: When performance data cannot be measured for the stated objectives, proxies may be used, such as the average duration of a task, response time or counts of errors.

q: A released product is not delivering the expected value. Interviews reveal nothing. Which technique may uncover that users have invented workarounds?
options: Document analysis
Benchmarking
Observation
Weighted ranking
explanation: Direct observation of users doing their work may uncover workarounds they use to compensate for product gaps. These can be missed in interviews, because long-standing users may not think to mention them.

q: What is the output of Evaluate Solution Performance, and what is it used for?
options: An assessment of business value, used for decisions to enhance, maintain, replace or discontinue the product
A stakeholder register, used for planning communication
A situation statement, used to start elicitation
A charter, used to authorize the project
explanation: The assessment of business value compares expected with actual value and the reasons for the difference. It is used to decide whether to develop a new product or to enhance, retire or discontinue an existing one.

q: Evaluation shows that the remaining planned features would add very little value for their cost. What may the organization do?
options: Build them anyway because they were planned
Double the team
Rewrite the business case to hide the result
End early and move the funds to higher-value work
explanation: Evaluation may identify a point of diminishing returns. Solution evaluation gives teams the ability to end early, even if more functionality could be built, so funds can go to higher-priority work.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Solution Evaluation
